content: The Philippines has a focus on bioethics and research ethics, with contributions from experts such as Ms. Terrie Wefwafwa. In Kenya, particularly in Nairobi, there is significant work being done on nutrition policies, legislation, and their implementation. Guidelines have been developed for infant feeding in areas affected by Zika virus transmission. Annex 6 includes systematic reviews conducted by various research teams. The first systematic review, led by Centeno-Tablante E., Medina-Rivera M., Finkelstein J.L., Herman H.S., Rayco-Solon P., Garcia-Casal M.N., Rogers L., Ghezzi-Kopel K., Zambrano Leal M.P., Andrade Velasquez J.K., Chang Asinc J.G., Peña-Rosas J.P., and Mehta S., provides an update on the transmission of the Zika virus through breast milk and breastfeeding. This review, published in Viruses in 2021, synthesizes evidence on this topic. The second systematic review, authored by Carroll C., Booth A., Campbell F., and Relton C., examines the implications of the Zika virus for infant feeding. This synthesis of qualitative evidence focuses on congenital Zika syndrome (CZS) and similar conditions. It was published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2020. The third systematic review, conducted by Martinez S.S., Pardo-Hernandez H., and Palacios C., explores feeding modifications and additional primary caregiver support for infants exposed to the Zika virus or diagnosed with congenital Zika syndrome. This rapid review of evidence was published in Tropical Medicine & International Health in 2020. The fourth systematic review, also by Carroll C., Booth A., Campbell F., and Relton C., synthesizes qualitative evidence on values and preferences to inform infant feeding in the context of non-HIV transmission risks. This work was published in PLoS One in 2020. Annex 7 acknowledges the contributions of peer reviewers, including Dr. Natalia Aragon Velez from Universidad del Valle in Cali, Colombia; Dr. Adriana Benavides from INCIESA in San Jose, Costa Rica; Dr. Pierre Buekens from the Center for Emerging Reproductive and Perinatal Epidemiology at Tulane University in New Orleans, USA; Dr. Erica Ota from St. Luke’s International University in Tokyo, Japan; Ms. Diana Valencia from the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in Atlanta, USA; and Dr. Stanley Zlotkin from the University of Toronto’s Hospital for Sick Children in Canada. It is noted that their acknowledgment does not imply endorsement of the guideline recommendations or represent the views of their affiliated institutions. Annex 8 lists members of the WHO Secretariat involved in the development of these guidelines. These include Dr. Madhava Ram Balakrishnan, Medical Officer for Global Vaccine Safety; Ms. Virginia Benassi, Technical Officer for Agenda, Policy, and Strategy; Dr. Ivana Knezevic, Team Leader for Technologies, Standards, and Norms; Dr. Marie Pierre Preziosi, Medical Officer for Agenda, Policy, and Strategy; Dr. Lisa Rogers, Technical Officer in the Department of Nutrition and Food Safety; and Ms. Rosa Seminario, Administrative Assistant in the Department of Nutrition and Food Safety.
